lead: Classification puts an embedded system into a named group so you can talk about it, pick tools for it, and judge whether a design fits. Three independent axes do most of the work: complexity, timing strictness, and physical form or connectivity. A washing-machine controller and an airbag controller can both be small boxes, yet only the airbag is hard real-time. These labels appear in datasheets, job interviews, and design reviews to set expectations before code is written.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the definition and example devices.

blocks.text: The first axis asks how much computing the product needs. Word size — the number of bits the processor handles in one go, such as 8-bit or 32-bit — is a useful proxy. It sets the address range, the arithmetic width, and how much memory the chip can easily reach. A small system uses an 8-bit microcontroller unit (MCU), a few kilobytes (KB) of flash for the program, and no operating system. A medium system uses a 16-bit or 32-bit processor and a small real-time operating system (RTOS) to manage several tasks. A large system uses a 32-bit or 64-bit system-on-chip (SoC), megabytes of RAM, and an embedded Linux or Android stack.

The table shows the usual split. Some syllabi call the classes small, medium and large; others call them type A, type B and type C. The names change, the idea does not: match the computing class to the job, not to fashion.
A small home router built on a 32-bit MCU with an RTOS is medium. A bank-branch 4G router running embedded Linux is large. The class follows the actual processor and OS, not the product name.
Word size is not a quality score. An 8-bit controller can be the correct and cheaper answer for a fixed job.

The second axis asks what happens when the system is late. A deadline is the latest time by which a result must be ready. In a hard real-time system, a missed deadline is a system failure. An airbag that fires 20 ms after the deadline, or an anti-lock braking system (ABS) that misses a 5 ms control loop, has failed in the safety sense. Hard does not mean fast in everyday terms; it means the deadline is not negotiable.

items: Hard: miss = failure. Examples: airbag, ABS, pacemaker.
Firm: late result is worthless but harmless. Example: one dropped video frame.
Soft: late result is still useful, only degraded. Example: a sluggish display refresh.

blocks.text: The complexity class and the timing class answer different questions. A small 8-bit MCU that must cut power within 10 ms of an over-current trip is hard real-time; a 64-bit tablet that feels fast is soft real-time. A device can be medium complexity and hard real-time, as the ABS example shows. Keep the two labels separate in an exam answer.

The third axis describes where the computer sits and how it talks. A standalone system is one box that works alone, such as a digital wristwatch. A distributed or networked system has many nodes sharing a bus or a wireless link; a bank branch 4G router, a car with controller area network (CAN) nodes, and a sensor mesh are examples. A mobile system is carried by a person or vehicle and usually runs on a battery, so power and size dominate.

Two more labels appear in syllabi. By generation, systems are called 4-bit, 8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit or 64-bit, following the processor word size. By implementation platform, systems are microcontroller-based (MCU), digital signal processor-based (DSP), field-programmable gate array-based (FPGA) or SoC-based. Chapter 1.5 explains how those platforms are chosen.

Use only the axes the question asks for. If a question says 'classify', name the axis first, then the class, then the reason. 'Medium, hard real-time, because a 5 ms loop miss loses braking control' is a complete answer.

spec.title: Three ways to classify
spec.aria: A tree with the root ES splitting into three branches — complexity, timing and form — each with two or three named leaves per branch.

examples.question: Classify each device on the complexity axis and the timing axis, and give the reason: (a) digital wristwatch, (b) ABS brake controller with a 5 ms control loop, (c) washing machine controller, (d) 4G router in a bank branch, (e) airbag controller that must fire within 20 ms of impact detection. Also state how many devices are hard real-time and how many are small.
steps: (a) Digital wristwatch: small complexity — an 8-bit MCU with no OS runs a fixed display job. Soft timing — a late display update is harmless.
(b) ABS brake controller: medium complexity — a 32-bit MCU with an RTOS manages a control loop. Hard timing — a missed 5 ms loop loses braking control.
(c) Washing machine controller: small complexity — an 8-bit MCU with no OS. Soft timing — a slow spin is only annoying.
(d) 4G router in a bank branch: large complexity — a 32-bit or 64-bit SoC with embedded Linux handles many flows. Soft timing and networked — delivery is best-effort and many nodes connect.
(e) Airbag controller: medium complexity — a dedicated MCU with a tight control task. Hard timing — a 20 ms miss is a safety failure.
Count hard real-time devices: (b) and (e), so 2 devices.
Count small devices: (a) and (c), so 2 devices.
examples.answer: The two hard real-time devices are (b) and (e); the two small devices are (a) and (c).
examples.check:
devices = [
    ('wristwatch', 'small', 'soft'),
    ('ABS', 'medium', 'hard'),
    ('washing machine', 'small', 'soft'),
    ('4G router', 'large', 'soft'),
    ('airbag', 'medium', 'hard'),
]
hard = sum(1 for d in devices if d[2] == 'hard')
small = sum(1 for d in devices if d[1] == 'small')
print(hard)
print(small)

traps: Hard real-time does not mean large or fast. A small 8-bit controller can be hard real-time; a 64-bit tablet is usually soft.
Firm and soft are not the same. A dropped video frame is firm (worthless), while a slow screen refresh is soft (still useful).
Networked does not imply large. A small sensor node with a radio is networked and small.
Word size is not a score. An 8-bit MCU can be the correct design for a fixed job.
Do not mix axes. 'Medium' answers complexity; 'hard' answers timing. Give both when asked to classify.

quiz.q: Name the three independent classification axes in this chapter.
Why is a 64-bit tablet usually soft real-time even though it is fast?
quiz.a: Its deadlines are human-facing; a late screen refresh or app response degrades experience but does not cause system failure. Speed does not make a deadline hard; the consequence of missing it does.

quiz.q: A printer uses a 32-bit MCU, a small RTOS, and must feed paper within 2 ms or jam. Classify it on complexity and timing axes.
quiz.a: Medium complexity (32-bit MCU, small RTOS). Firm real-time: a late sheet feed produces a worthless page, but the machine is not destroyed and the job can be restarted. It is hard real-time only if the miss causes an unrecoverable failure, such as a head crash or a safety hazard.

quiz.q: Explain why complexity class and timing class are independent. Give one counterexample in each direction.
quiz.a: A small 8-bit MCU that must trip a relay within 10 ms of over-current detection is hard real-time, so small does not mean soft. A large 64-bit tablet is soft, so large does not mean hard. The axes answer different questions: how much computing, and what a late result costs.
A system where a late result is worthless but harmless, such as a dropped video frame.

quiz.q: A video player drops one frame when it cannot decode in time. Which timing class is this?
quiz.a: Firm, because the late frame is useless but no failure occurs.

quiz.q: A hospital wants a networked electrocardiogram (ECG) monitor. Which classification axes matter, and what would you ask before choosing a class?
quiz.a: Timing matters first: is a missed alarm hard real-time? Complexity matters for signal processing and display; connectivity matters because it is networked. Ask the deadline and the consequence of a miss before naming the class.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, these labels drive procurement: a hard real-time claim changes the processor, the RTOS, and the test plan. Researchers use the same axes when they describe cyber-physical systems and edge nodes. Newer curricula add 'AI at the edge' as a complexity class, but the timing and form axes still apply.
